Okay, to paraphrase Ronway from memory:

* Batman is primarily a melee combatant while Wraith is mostly ranged.

* Wraith's parents are still alive, but criminals didn't attack Batman himself.

* Wraith makes little apparent effort to intimidate her foes; Bruce Wayne became Batman because he figured bats were frightening, but Maia whatsername became the Wraith because being stealthy made her feel safer, enabling her to fight crime and thereby make herself safer still.  (Debatably, as a victim of violent crime herself, Wraith might have more of an ethical objection to terrifying or unnecessarily brutalizing the crooks she's taking down than Batman appears to, though of course Batman's attitudes vary wildly as different writers get a hold of him.)

* Wraith doesn't drive a Wraithmobile (as far as we know), but Batman doesn't usually turn household appliances into his iconic weapons.

* Though I haven't personally seen much evidence of this, Ronway also claims that Wraith has responded very positively to her membership in the Freedom #, whereas Batman's membership in the Justice League has always been sort of grudging and utilitarian...he would rather work alone, if he didn't need the League's help or they his, whereas Ronway opines that Wraith actively likes being a team player.  (Which would make sense, given that SOTM is a team game; I picture Expatriette as being pretty much of a loner, but in general it's reasonable to assume that few of the characters of a cooperative game would turn up their nose at collaborating with their colleagues, even on relatively nonessential matters.)

McBehrer:

5; Dragged into the Underworld (or whatever it's called) is destroyed if there are (H) trials in play, Urshe pulls out (H) cards from the environment deck, the spike trap (I think) deal (H) damage, etc.

Actually it's a more complicated question than that.  The swinging blades trap (not the spike trap) only deals H-based damage if you intentionally put yourself in front of the blade to stop it…its automatic damage is a flat 3 every turn.  More, the Challenge of Fire is extremely easy to get rid of in a five-hero game (five players must discard 7 cards between them, which is generally pretty easy unless you're playing Nightmist or Bunker, fighting Citizen Dawn or Iron Legacy or the like, or have been suffering from a Swarm of Scarabs for quite some time), while with H=3, it levies a fairly stiff fine (at least one player MUST discard the full 3 cards, which is often quite a sacrifice, and no more than one player can fail to discard at all, or else the fire will keep coming - not that any of Ra's buddies will mind, of course, but otherwise it's pretty painful).  5 is probably still the correct number because of the two cards you mention, but there's really only them and the Challenge, and with a 1/15 chance versus a 2/15 chance that you'll regret having either 3 or 5 heroes, I can see an argument for 3 and perhaps even for 4, which might be the best or the worst of both worlds.  (Had I been involved in playtesting for IR, I would certainly have pushed for there to be another card which punishes H = 3 to balance things out more equally, but that's only one of the changes I'd have suggested making.)
